title: Narada's equanimity
hookLine: the great Brahma Narada helps a king back to good sense with calm (Jataka 544)
tomorrow: ten perfections. which one do you need most right now?

cards: Somebody at the dinner table has decided that nothing anyone does really matters, so why bother. You can feel the table getting ready for a fight. An old Jataka starts right there.
King Angati takes a teacher's word that deeds bear no fruit: good or bad, nothing comes back. So he stops giving, and lets his duties slide. His daughter, Ruja, pleads with him, and he won't hear it.
Then, the story says, the great Brahma Narada comes down from his heaven, dressed as a wandering ascetic, to talk with the king. Not to shout him down. To talk.

teach.b: So, the question: how do you help someone back to good sense? The Jataka's answer is in how Narada talks. In this story he is a great Brahma, a god.
He could thunder. He doesn't. He reasons with the king, patiently, shows him where careless deeds lead, and stays level when the king pushes back.
And the king comes back to good sense. Tradition tells this as the life in which the Bodhisatta perfected equanimity.
Calm helps, because a calm voice leaves the other person room to turn around without losing face. A neighbor tradition says nearly the same thing in one line.

The book of Proverbs, in the Hebrew Bible, which Jews and Christians both read: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." That's what they share: the calm voice is the one that gets through.

teach.h: REVERENCE FOR GOD; DEEDS AND PRACTICE.
teach.b: Proverbs roots wisdom in reverence for God: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge," it says near its start.

In the Jataka, Narada's calm is a perfection trained over many lives, and what he points the king toward is the fruit of the king's own deeds. One grounds wisdom in God; the other in cause and effect and long practice.
Each is whole in its own house.

how: The Mahanaradakassapa Jataka is among the great birth stories retold and painted in Theravada temples, and Buddhists cultivate equanimity in meditation as one of the four divine abodes.

o: a calm that helps someone back to good sense
a god's anger at a king who did wrong
staying silent while others argue it out

games.q: who's who at the king's court — tap the pairs.
p: his daughter, who pleaded with him
a great Brahma who stayed calm
a soft answer turns away wrath

s: equanimity means staying out of other people's mistakes
Narada stepped in; his calm is what made the help work.
in the story, Narada is a great Brahma, a god
he could have thundered; he reasoned calmly instead.
staying calm means agreeing, so nobody gets upset
Narada disagreed with the king completely, and calmly.

games.q: your uncle insists at dinner that being honest never pays, so why bother. the table is tensing up. what would Narada do?
o: reason with him calmly, and ask where honesty has paid off for him.
out-argue him loudly, so everyone sees he's wrong.
change the subject; equanimity means staying out of it.
games.why: Narada didn't stay out of it or thunder. he reasoned, level and patient, and the king came back to good sense.

practice: Close your eyes and bring back the last time someone near you was upset. Don't replay the argument.
Feel your feet on the floor and your breath going out, and find the voice you'd want to answer with: lower, slower, with room in it.

wordCard.voice: Narada's equanimity: the great Brahma's level calm, which helped a king back to good sense without a fight.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: Narada, the great Brahma of Jataka 544, told as the Bodhisatta.

carryVoice: Keep this one: calm helps, because a soft answer leaves room to turn around. Twenty-nine of thirty.
